label: boomer
source_text: [Pew] By this definition, both are shorter than the span of the Baby Boomers (19 years) – the only generation officially designated by the U.S. Census Bureau, based on the famous surge in post-WWII births in 1946 and a significant decline in birthrates after 1964. [...] [Wikipedia, Baby boomers] Theirs was a time of economic prosperity and rapid technological progress, and many grew up expecting the world to improve with time. However, young people felt a sense of alienation and sought to assert their own individuality, freedom, and authenticity. [...] [Wikipedia, OK boomer] The phrase has developed into a retort for resistance to technological change, climate change denial, marginalization of members of minority groups, or opposition to younger generations' values more generally. [...] [Wikipedia, Baby boomers] In the West, those born in the years before the actual boom were often the most influential people among boomers. Some of these people were musicians such as The Beatles, Bob Dylan, and The Rolling Stones A significant cultural event of this era was the Woodstock Festival in August 1969, which drew huge crowds despite bad weather and a general lack of facilities. [...] [Word Smarts, 'Everything Is Groovy With This Boomer Slang'] As children and teens during the ’60s and ’70s, boomers came up with some of the grooviest words to boogie down to. While many of these haven’t stood the test of time, other terms remain fresh. Groovy Fashionable and exciting; enjoyable and excellent. [...] [Word Smarts, 'These Slang Terms Reveal Which Generation You Were Born In'] Baby boomers (born between 1946 and 1964) embraced slang on a wider scale, coining sayings such as “boob tube” (“television”), “threads” (“clothing”), and “ticked off” (“annoyed”), to name just a few. Boomers also came up with “dig it” for when you’re really into something, or saying you have to “split” when it’s time to leave. Other slang words from this time include “groovy” (“cool”), “square” (“uncool”), and “moo juice,” to describe a fresh glass of milk. [...] [Babbel, 'Talkin’ ‘Bout The Generations: Baby Boomer Language'] Words and phrases like “groovy” and “boogie” and “space cadet” all reached the heights of mainstream success in those decades, when baby boomers were becoming teen boomers. That also explains why baby boomers are often the people resisting linguistic changes introduced by the younger generations (the overuse of “like,” the non-literal “literally” and vocal fry are all common targets for baby boomers). [...] [Word Smarts, 'How Your Punctuation Habits Reveal Your Age'] millennials have a habit of ending sentences with "lol," while baby boomers might trail off with an ellipsis ("How are you…"). Baby boomers, for example, are known for their love of ellipses. They're everywhere: to end a sentence, to soften the tone, or to indicate trailing thoughts. Less than one-quarter of Gen Z respondents use punctuation in casual communication, while more than half of baby boomers (55%) report always using it while texting or posting online. Meanwhile, only 16% of Gen Z and 28% of millennials consistently use periods at the end of sentences. [...] [Wikipedia, A group where we all pretend to be boomers] A group where we all pretend to be boomers is a Facebook group created in May 2019, for users – the majority of whom are millennials and in Generation Z – to pretend to be baby boomers. Members of the group post in character as a stereotypical baby boomer. The style of speech used in the group has been termed a register called "boomerspeak" by linguist Gretchen McCulloch. Examples of this manner of speech include posts with spelling mistakes, posts written in all capitals, non sequiturs, and the large use of GIFs of Minions. Due to older people more readily sharing fake news on Facebook, many members ironically post fake news in the group, in imitation. [...] [Pew, 'Millennials stand out for their technology use' (2019)] More than nine-in-ten Millennials (93% of those who turn ages 23 to 38 this year) own smartphones, compared with 90% of Gen Xers (those ages 39 to 54 this year), 68% of Baby Boomers (ages 55 to 73) and 40% of the Silent Generation (74 to 91) around three-fourths or more of both Millennials and Gen Xers now report using Facebook (84% vs. 74%, respectively). Boomers and Silents have both increased their Facebook use by double digits since 2015.
description_draft: This means being born between 1946 and 1964: raised on the Beatles and Woodstock, still saying 'groovy', posting on Facebook in all caps with ellipses and Minion memes, and resisting technological change and younger generations' values.
nearest_existing: elderly / nostalgic / late_adopter / traditional: elderly is age alone (seventies or beyond); the typed version is a birth cohort (about 62 to 80 in 2026) with the stereotyped postwar optimism, sixties individualism, and resistance to new technology and to younger generations' values.
notes: Roger, 2026-10-07: the generation descriptions carry the cohort's stereotyped speech, slang and culture, and voice is wanted here; the 36-word allowance applies to the set. Each v2 draft keeps Pew's birth years and the v1 portrait traits that fit, and adds markers of three kinds: a characteristic word or phrase, a medium or habit of communication, a cultural touchstone. Sources that name the cohort and the words explicitly were preferred; the dictionary publishers were out of reach (Merriam-Webster's slang pages and its 'OK boomer' piece sit behind a bot check, HTTP 403; Dictionary.com's article links redirect to a generic index), so the word-level sources are Word Smarts (three generation-labelled slang pieces and a punctuation piece), Mental Floss and Babbel, with Wikipedia and Pew for the media habits and touchstones. All v1 source pieces are kept; every new piece is checked verbatim against the raw page. Markers: 'the Beatles and Woodstock' from Wikipedia 'Baby boomers' (the most influential people among boomers; the Woodstock Festival as the era's significant cultural event); 'groovy' from Word Smarts' boomer-slang piece, Word Smarts' generations piece and Babbel's boomer piece (all three name boomers and the word); 'posting on Facebook in all caps with ellipses and Minion memes' from Wikipedia's article on the parody group (posts in all capitals, spelling mistakes, non sequiturs, GIFs of Minions, 'boomerspeak') plus Word Smarts' punctuation piece (boomers trail off with an ellipsis, known for their love of ellipses) and Pew 2019 (Boomers' Facebook use up by double digits; 68% own smartphones); 'resisting technological change and younger generations' values' from Wikipedia 'OK boomer', with Babbel's 'resisting linguistic changes introduced by the younger generations' behind it. Dropped from v1 for room: 'growing up in postwar prosperity expecting the world to keep improving' and 'prizing individuality and freedom'. Climate denial and marginalization of minorities (OK boomer list) still left out as the sharpest items. Strength: the Facebook stereotype comes from an article about a parody group that imitates 'a stereotypical internet user from the baby boomer generation', i.e. it is a stereotype by the source's own account; the draft states it as the person's habit, which is the voice Roger asked for. 36 words.
set_review: Sequence in birth order, v2 with speech and culture. Each draft still opens 'This means being born between <years>' with Pew's years, then two or three markers of the agreed kinds and the v1 portrait traits that fit: boomer = Beatles/Woodstock, 'groovy', Facebook all-caps/ellipses/Minion memes, resistance to change; gen-x = empty house after school, MTV and grunge, eye-rolls and 'as if', independent/skeptical/unconcerned; millennial = AOL Instant Messenger/Myspace/Harry Potter, recession and student debt, avocado toast, 'adulting', confident/tolerant/entitled; gen-z = YouTube/TikTok, smartphone in hand, 'no cap'/'slay', texting without periods, better behaved, open about mental health. Lengths 34 to 36, within the 36 allowance Roger granted for this set. The markers are stereotypes by design and the sources say so (parody group, 'became a stereotype of the millennial generation', 'This type became a stereotype for members of Generation X'); strength mirrored, and the millennial 'entitled' is in by Roger's decision. Caveat on authority: the word-level sources are popular-press slang pieces (Word Smarts, Mental Floss, Babbel) because the dictionary publishers were unreachable; the media habits and touchstones are Wikipedia and Pew. 'Whatever', the Gen X word most often cited, had no reachable cohort-naming source (HowStuffWorks returned an empty bot-check page), so the Gen X phrase is 'as if' (Clueless, 1995), which Word Smarts attributes to Gen X explicitly.

label: gen-x
source_text: [Pew] Generation X (born between 1965 and 1980) [...] [Wikipedia] As children in the 1970s and 1980s, a time of shifting societal values, Gen Xers were sometimes called the "Latchkey Generation", a reference to their returning as children from school to an empty home Xers were dubbed the "MTV Generation" (a reference to the music video channel) and sometimes characterized as slackers, cynical, and disaffected. [...] In 2014, Pew Research provided further insight, describing the cohort as "savvy, skeptical and self-reliant; they're not into preening or pampering, and they just might not give much of a hoot what others think of them. [...] guides regarding managing multiple generations in the workforce describe Gen Xers as: independent, resilient, resourceful, self-managing, adaptable, cynical, pragmatic, skeptical of authority, and as seeking a work-life balance. [...] [Wikipedia, Generation X] Video games, via both arcades and home consoles, were also a major part of childhood entertainment for the first time among Xers. Nirvana singer Kurt Cobain (pictured here in 1992) was called the "voice of Generation X" in the 1990s, playing the same role for this demographic as Bob Dylan and John Lennon played for baby boomers in the 1960s. [...] [Wikipedia, Slacker] "Slacker" became widely used in the 1990s to refer to a type of apathetic youth who were cynical and uninterested in political or social causes. This type became a stereotype for members of Generation X. [...] [Word Smarts, '8 Gnarly Slang Terms Made Popular by Generation X'] Born between baby boomers and millennials, the members of Generation X are marked by unique cultural influences, a rebellious spirit, and distinctive language. This phrase is a great catchall to demonstrate disbelief, skepticism, or dismissiveness, and it works especially well with an eye roll. The 1995 movie Clueless popularized “as if” for the masses, though director Amy Heckerling credits the slang to the LQBTQ+ community Dude For Gen Xers, a dude can be anyone — the word has evolved to be somewhat of a gender-neutral noun. [...] [Word Smarts, 'These Slang Terms Reveal Which Generation You Were Born In'] Generation X includes anyone born from 1965 through 1980. Gen Xers are known for living a somewhat grungier lifestyle than their predecessors, as evidenced by the music that became popular in the late 1980s and early ’90s. This generation popularized terms such as “gnarly” and “phat.” “This rocks” describes something that’s amazing, and slang terms including “dude” and “homeslice” became positive terms of address. [...] [Mental Floss, 'Words Gen X Made Popular'] Gen X, the demographic born between the years 1965 and 1980, was often depicted as relaxed, cynical, and music-loving at their cultural peak in the 1980s and ’90s —and plenty of the slang they used reflects that. [...] [Pew, 'Millennials stand out for their technology use' (2019)] More than nine-in-ten Millennials (93% of those who turn ages 23 to 38 this year) own smartphones, compared with 90% of Gen Xers (those ages 39 to 54 this year), 68% of Baby Boomers (ages 55 to 73) and 40% of the Silent Generation (74 to 91) around three-fourths or more of both Millennials and Gen Xers now report using Facebook (84% vs. 74%, respectively). Boomers and Silents have both increased their Facebook use by double digits since 2015.
description_draft: This means being born between 1965 and 1980: coming home to an empty house after school, raised on MTV and grunge, answering with eye-rolls and 'as if', independent, skeptical of authority and unconcerned what others think.
nearest_existing: independent / self_reliant / cynical / skeptical: the typed version is the cohort (about 46 to 61 in 2026) with the latchkey childhood and the slacker-skeptic image; plain cynical is distrust of human nature, which the typed version does not claim, and plain self_reliant sees a team as dead weight, which it does not.

Each v2 draft keeps Pew's birth years and the v1 portrait traits that fit, and adds markers of three kinds: a characteristic word or phrase, a medium or habit of communication, a cultural touchstone. Sources that name the cohort and the words explicitly were preferred; the dictionary publishers were out of reach (Merriam-Webster's slang pages and its 'OK boomer' piece sit behind a bot check, HTTP 403; Dictionary.com's article links redirect to a generic index), so the word-level sources are Word Smarts (three generation-labelled slang pieces and a punctuation piece), Mental Floss and Babbel, with Wikipedia and Pew for the media habits and touchstones. All v1 source pieces are kept; every new piece is checked verbatim against the raw page. Markers: 'empty house after school' from Wikipedia 'Generation X' (the latchkey sentence, v1); 'MTV' from the same article's 'MTV Generation' sentence (the channel named, not the nickname); 'grunge' from Wikipedia 'Generation X' (Kurt Cobain called the 'voice of Generation X'; grunge among the genres) and Word Smarts' generations piece ('a somewhat grungier lifestyle'); 'answering with eye-rolls and "as if"' from Word Smarts' Gen X slang piece ('as if' demonstrates disbelief, skepticism, or dismissiveness, 'works especially well with an eye roll', popularized by Clueless, 1995); the portrait traits from v1 (Wikipedia's workforce-guide list and Pew 2014 as quoted there). Not used: 'dude' (Word Smarts, Mental Floss; less specific to the cohort), 'slacker' (Wikipedia 'Slacker': a stereotype for Gen X; the eye-roll clause carries the attitude), arcade and console games (Wikipedia; no room), the French 'Génération Bof' ('bof' = 'whatever'; about France). Strength: Mental Floss's 'relaxed, cynical, and music-loving' and Wikipedia's 'slackers, cynical, and disaffected' are the source level; the draft stays there. 36 words.

label: millennial
source_text: [Pew] Anyone born between 1981 and 1996 (ages 23 to 38 in 2019) is considered a Millennial, and anyone born from 1997 onward is part of a new generation. [...] [Wikipedia] elevated familiarity with the Internet and technology in general, and usage of early social media platforms such as AOL Instant Messenger, LiveJournal, and Myspace. [...] Twenge attributes millennials with the traits of confidence and tolerance, but also describes a sense of entitlement and narcissism [...] with many facing high levels of youth unemployment, student debt, and childcare costs in the wake of the Great Recession [...] Across the globe, millennials and subsequent generations have postponed marriage or living together as a couple. [...] [Wikipedia, Millennials] Second-wave millennials are nostalgic for the childhood culture of the early 2000s, such as SpongeBob SquarePants, Samurai Jack, Kim Possible, Pokemon, Lizzie McGuire, the Harry Potter series, and the Game Boy Advance. In 2008, author Ron Alsop called the millennials "Trophy Kids", a term that reflects a trend in competitive sports, as well as many other aspects of life, where mere participation is frequently enough for a reward. Many millennial parents document the childhood and growth of their children on social media platforms such as Instagram and Facebook. [...] [Wikipedia, Avocado toast] In Australia in late 2016, consumption of avocado smashed on toast became a target of criticism after columnist Bernard Salt in The Australian wrote an article about how "young people order smashed avocado with crumbled feta on five-grain toasted bread at $22 a pop and more", arguing that they should be saving to buy a house instead. The article made headlines internationally and became a stereotype of the millennial generation. Tim Gurner, a 35-year-old Australian property developer, stated in May 2017 that millennials should not be buying smashed avocado and $4 lattes in their pursuit of home ownership. [...] [Mental Floss, 'Millennial Slang: 16 Terms You Should Totes Know'] If you still use terms like adulting, doggo, and YOLO, you may be a Millennial. These terms popularized by the generation were inescapable in the 2000s and 2010s. As the youngest millennials entered young adulthood over the next decade , the term exploded in popularity. Though it often appears in a tongue-in-cheek context, it’s been used to reinforce negative stereotypes of Millennials being lazy and immature. [...] [Word Smarts, 'These Slang Terms Reveal Which Generation You Were Born In'] Millennials, the more popular term for Gen Y, are people born from 1981 to 1996. The rise of this generation coincided with the rise of the internet, so many slang terms are the initialisms that developed out of internet culture: “BRB” (“be right back”), “OMG” (“oh my god”), “TBH” (“to be honest”), among others. Millennials are also responsible for coining words such as “bae” (to talk about their significant other) and “slay” (to praise someone doing something exceptionally well). You may also hear a millennial use “adulting” when behaving responsibly, “keeping it 100” when being real and truthful, or “getting swole” when lifting weights at the gym. This generation may also feel serious “FOMO,” which means a “fear of missing out.” [...] [Word Smarts, 'How Your Punctuation Habits Reveal Your Age'] millennials have a habit of ending sentences with "lol," while baby boomers might trail off with an ellipsis ("How are you…"). [...] [Pew, 'Millennials: Confident. Connected. Open to Change' (2010)] They embrace multiple modes of self-expression. Three-quarters have created a profile on a social networking site. One-in-five have posted a video of themselves online. Nearly four-in-ten have a tattoo [...] [Pew, 'Millennials stand out for their technology use' (2019)] Similarly, the vast majority of Millennials (86%) say they use social media, compared with smaller shares among older generations. around three-fourths or more of both Millennials and Gen Xers now report using Facebook (84% vs. 74%, respectively). Boomers and Silents have both increased their Facebook use by double digits since 2015.
description_draft: This means being born between 1981 and 1996: raised on AOL Instant Messenger, Myspace and Harry Potter, entering work in a recession with student debt, brunching on avocado toast, calling chores 'adulting', confident, tolerant and entitled.
nearest_existing: confident / plugged_in / financially_precarious / early_adopter: the typed version is the cohort (about 30 to 45 in 2026) shaped by the internet's arrival and the 2008 recession; plugged_in is on the feeds all day at any age, financially_precarious is a present condition not a cohort history.

Sources that name the cohort and the words explicitly were preferred; the dictionary publishers were out of reach (Merriam-Webster's slang pages and its 'OK boomer' piece sit behind a bot check, HTTP 403; Dictionary.com's article links redirect to a generic index), so the word-level sources are Word Smarts (three generation-labelled slang pieces and a punctuation piece), Mental Floss and Babbel, with Wikipedia and Pew for the media habits and touchstones. All v1 source pieces are kept; every new piece is checked verbatim against the raw page. Markers: 'AOL Instant Messenger, Myspace' from Wikipedia 'Millennials' (early social media platforms, v1 piece); 'Harry Potter' from the same article's nostalgia sentence (second-wave millennials; the Harry Potter series); 'recession with student debt' from Wikipedia and Pew 2019 (v1); 'brunching on avocado toast' from Wikipedia 'Avocado toast' (Salt's column 'became a stereotype of the millennial generation'; Gurner on smashed avocado and $4 lattes); 'calling chores "adulting"' from Mental Floss ('If you still use terms like adulting, doggo, and YOLO, you may be a Millennial') and Word Smarts' generations piece ('adulting' when behaving responsibly); 'confident, tolerant and entitled' from Wikipedia's Twenge sentence, 'entitled' now in by Roger's decision (Mental Floss adds that 'adulting' reinforces the lazy-and-immature stereotype). label: gen-z
source_text: [Pew] anyone born from 1997 onward is part of a new generation The iPhone launched in 2007, when the oldest Gen Zers were 10. Social media, constant connectivity and on-demand entertainment and communication are innovations Millennials adapted to as they came of age. For those born after 1996, these are largely assumed. [...] [Wikipedia] with the generation typically being defined as people born from 1997 to 2012. Generation Z has been described as "better behaved and less hedonistic" than previous generations. They have fewer teenage pregnancies, consume less alcohol (but not necessarily less of other psychoactive drugs), and are more focused on school and job prospects. [...] There is greater awareness and diagnosis of mental health conditions among Generation Z, and sleep deprivation is more frequently reported. [...] [Wikipedia, Generation Z] Many slang terms of Generations Z and Alpha—such as flex, no cap, slay, or shade—have their roots in African-American vernacular English, and, thanks to the Internet, spread much more rapidly than they otherwise would. At the same time, YouTube has claimed the top spot while Snapchat and Instagram have also made significant gains. During the late 2010s and early 2020s, TikTok exploded in usage among adolescents and has become the second most frequently used platform, surpassing Instagram in 2021. Having a mobile device has become almost universal by the time the first wave of Generation Z reaches adolescence, to such an extent that it is common for them to feel uncomfortable or unsafe without one Speed and reliability are important factors in their choice of social networking platform, and they make frequent use of emojis. [...] [Wikipedia, Glossary of 2020s slang] English-language slang used or popularized in the 2020s, usually by Generation Z or by Generation Alpha, differs from that of earlier generations. cap To lie originating from AAVE. The antonym, "no cap", is typically used after a statement to indicate truthfulness or being genuine. slay To do something well. bussin' Extremely good, excellent. it's giving Used to describe an attitude or connotation. [...] [Word Smarts, 'These Slang Terms Reveal Which Generation You Were Born In'] Gen Zers, also known as “zoomers,” came into the world between 1997 and 2012. For many older adults today, Gen Z slang is enough to make your head spin. But terms such as “cheugy” (“outdated”) and “sus” (“questionable” or “dishonest”) are part of a coded language that these young people share. Another popular series of terms coined by this generation are “cap” (“false”), “no cap” (“true”), and “capping” (“lying”). [...] [Word Smarts, 'How Your Punctuation Habits Reveal Your Age'] Less than one-quarter of Gen Z respondents use punctuation in casual communication, while more than half of baby boomers (55%) report always using it while texting or posting online. Meanwhile, only 16% of Gen Z and 28% of millennials consistently use periods at the end of sentences. [...] [Wikipedia, OK boomer] The phrase first drew widespread attention due to a November 2019 TikTok video in response to an older man, though the phrase had been coined years before that.
description_draft: This means being born between 1997 and 2012: raised on YouTube and TikTok, smartphone in hand, saying 'no cap' and 'slay', texting without periods, better behaved than earlier teens, and open about mental health.
